g10-chemistry-uc4-t1.overview: Every chemical reaction trades energy — some warm their surroundings (burning fuel, hand warmers), some steal heat (cold packs, photosynthesis). This lesson measures those trades: exothermic vs endothermic, the energy-level diagram, and q = mcΔT arithmetic that turns a temperature change into joules.
objectives: Classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic with examples
Draw and interpret energy-level diagrams with activation energy
Explain bond breaking (energy in) and bond making (energy out)
Calculate heat change with q = mcΔT
g10-chemistry-uc4-t1.simple: Reactions come in two thermal flavours. EXOTHERMIC: releases heat → surroundings get WARMER → products sit at LOWER energy than reactants (ΔH negative): combustion, neutralisation, respiration, thermite, hand warmers. ENDOTHERMIC: absorbs heat → surroundings get COOLER → products at HIGHER energy (ΔH positive): photosynthesis, thermal decomposition, cold packs, baking soda + vinegar. Where does the energy go? BOND ACCOUNTING: breaking bonds COSTS energy, making bonds PAYS energy back — if the payback exceeds the cost, the reaction is exothermic (most fuels). Every reaction still needs a spark: ACTIVATION ENERGY — the upfront push to start breaking bonds (why paper needs a flame even though burning it releases more). Measure heat with q = mcΔT: mass × specific heat × temperature change (water's c = 4200 J/kg°C — it resists temperature change, which is why it makes a great calorimeter).
g10-chemistry-uc4-t1.detailed:
Energy diagrams: x-axis = reaction progress, y = stored chemical energy. Exothermic: reactants high → hump (activation energy Ea from reactants to peak) → products LOWER; ΔH = products − reactants < 0. Endothermic: products HIGHER, ΔH > 0. The hump is universal — even energy-releasing reactions need Ea to get going (match before candle catches). Catalysts lower the hump (see G11 kinetics) without changing ΔH.

Bond energy accounting: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds made). Broken costs, made pays. Example methane combustion: break 4 C-H (4×413) + 2 O=O (2×496) = 2644 kJ; make 2 C=O (2×743) + 4 O-H (4×463) = 3338 kJ → ΔH ≈ −694 kJ/mol (real value −890 — averages make it approximate). Exothermic = stronger bonds in products. Endothermic decomposition (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ needs continuous heating): pay exceeds payback.

Calorimetry math: q = mcΔT — m in kg, c water = 4200 J/(kg·°C), ΔT in °C (or K — same step). Assumptions: solution ≈ water's c, no heat loss (polystyrene cup + lid + stirrer minimises it), cup absorbs ~nothing. Per-mole: ΔH = −q/n (exothermic sign convention). Neutralisation: 50 mL 1 M HCl + 50 mL 1 M NaOH → ΔT ≈ +6.8 °C → q = 0.1 kg × 4200 × 6.8 = 2856 J for 0.05 mol → ΔH ≈ −57 kJ/mol (textbook −57.1 — your experiment will read low; heat loss is the systematic error). Displacement: excess Zn powder in CuSO₄ solution, lid on, ΔT up (Cu²⁺ + Zn → Cu + Zn²⁺ exothermic). Dissolution: NH₄NO₃ in water → temperature DROPS (endothermic — instant cold pack); NaOH pellets → rises sharply.

Where the energy physically lives: Chemical potential energy = electron arrangements and nuclear-electron attractions. Burning petrol: sunlight stored by ancient photosynthesis (endothermic then) released now (exothermic now) — fossil fuels are packaged solar energy. Respiration is the same glucose combustion in slow enzymatic steps at 37 °C.

workedExamples.problem: 50 mL of 2.0 M HCl at 19.5 °C is mixed with 50 mL of 2.0 M NaOH at 19.5 °C in a polystyrene cup; maximum temperature 32.3 °C. Calculate the heat released and ΔH per mole of water formed.
workedExamples.answer: −54 kJ/mol — close to the −57.1 literature value; the gap is heat loss.

workedExamples.problem: Using bond energies (C-H 413, O=O 496, C=O 743, O-H 463 kJ/mol), estimate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O and classify the reaction.
workedExamples.given: Bonds: 4 C-H + 2 O=O broken; 2 C=O + 4 O-H made.
workedExamples.answer: Negative → exothermic — combustion pays back more than it costs.

workedExamples.problem: When NH₄NO₃ dissolves in water the beaker gets cold and condensation forms underneath. Explain with energy terms and state the sign of ΔH.
workedExamples.formula: Dissolution balance: lattice breaking vs hydration.
workedExamples.substitution: Breaking the ionic lattice costs energy; hydrating the ions pays some back — for NH₄NO₃ the cost WINS → net energy absorbed from surroundings → water temperature falls → beaker exterior cools air below dew point → condensation. ΔH > 0 (endothermic dissolution).
workedExamples.calculation: Same logic: NaOH dissolution pays back more → hot.
workedExamples.answer: Endothermic (+ΔH) — 'cold' means the system stole heat from around it.

workedExamples.problem: A student heats 100 g of water and it needs 8400 J to rise 20 °C. Find c and predict the ΔT if the same heater ran twice as long on half the water.
workedExamples.answer: c = 4200; ΔT = 80 °C — double heat into half the mass = 4× the rise.

commonMistakes: Saying 'exothermic reactions don't need energy' — they need ACTIVATION energy to start (the hump), then pay back more.
Reading ΔT backwards: endothermic = surroundings COOL (temperature falls); the reaction itself absorbed.
Forgetting the minus sign: ΔH = −q/n for exothermic — students report +57 kJ/mol for neutralisation.
Using grams instead of kg in q = mcΔT with c = 4200 — factor-of-1000 error.
Thinking the products 'contain cold' — cold isn't a substance; heat FLOWED from surroundings into the reaction.
Assuming bond breaking releases energy — breaking ALWAYS costs; only bond MAKING pays.
Ignoring heat loss then wondering why school values (−54) beat literature (−57) — measured ΔT is always low.
Confusing 'temperature' with 'heat' — a spark has high temperature, a bath has more heat energy; ΔT is the thermometer reading, q is the joules.
applications: Instant cold packs: NH₄NO₃/urea + water — endothermic dissolution for sports injuries.
Hand warmers: crystallisation of sodium acetate (exothermic) or iron oxidation.
Fuel choice = energy accounting: compare kJ per gram or per birr — cooking gas vs charcoal vs firewood deforestation.
Building science: lime slaking (CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂) is strongly exothermic — site safety when mixing.
Body temperature: respiration's exothermic glucose oxidation keeps you at 37 °C — sweating is the exhaust system.
Refrigeration logic: endothermic evaporation of refrigerant steals heat from inside the box (and your injera stays fresh).
g10-chemistry-uc4-t1.summary: Exothermic: heat out, ΔH −, products lower (combustion, neutralisation, displacement). Endothermic: heat in, ΔH +, products higher (photosynthesis, decomposition, cold packs). Ea hump = the starting push. Bond math: broken − made. Measure: q = mcΔT (water c = 4200), ΔH = −q/n; heat loss makes results small.

steps.detail: Pay activation energy — climb the hump
steps.label: Push

pairs.q: Paper + oxygen is exothermic, yet a sheet just sits on a desk. Why?
pairs.a: Ea: room-temperature collisions can't clear the hump — a flame supplies the activation push, then it self-sustains.

pairs.q: Why does the beaker feel cold when NH₄NO₃ dissolves?
pairs.a: Lattice-breaking costs more than hydration pays → the solution steals heat from the glass and your hand.

pairs.q: Your neutralisation ΔH reads −54 not −57.1 kJ/mol. Name the error and its direction.
pairs.a: Heat loss to cup/air — systematic, always makes |ΔH| too small (insulate better, extrapolate cooling curves).

questions.q: Which is endothermic?
questions.explanation: Plants absorb light energy to build glucose.

questions.q: q (J) to warm 0.2 kg water by 5 °C? (c = 4200)
In an exothermic diagram, products are ____ reactants.
questions.explanation: Energy released = products sit lower.

questions.q: The minimum energy needed to start a reaction is ____ energy.
questions.explanation: The hump on every energy diagram.

questions.q: Is bond breaking exothermic or endothermic? Explain why making bonds is the opposite.
questions.explanation: Separating bonded atoms requires energy input; forming bonds releases that energy as the pair falls to lower energy.

questions.q: Broken = 2644 kJ, made = 3338 kJ. ΔH (kJ/mol)?
Exothermic reactions release more energy making bonds than they consume breaking them.
questions.explanation: That net payback IS the released heat.

questions.q: 100 mL solution rose 6.8 °C (c = 4200, ρ = 1 g/mL). q in J?
Why does condensation form UNDER a cold-pack beaker?
questions.answer: cools air below dew point|water vapour condenses|surroundings lost heat
questions.explanation: The endothermic dissolution cools the glass, which cools the air touching it — its water vapour condenses.

questions.q: Pick the correct calorimetry chain:
questions.explanation: Measure temperature, compute heat, divide by moles, apply sign.

g10-chemistry-uc4-t2.overview: Electrons can be made to flow on purpose. A GALVANIC cell turns a spontaneous redox reaction into usable current (batteries); ELECTROLYSIS forces current into a non-spontaneous reaction to split or plate substances (aluminium, electroplating, recharging). Both are the same chemistry pointed in opposite directions.
objectives: Describe a simple cell: two different metals, electrolyte, electron flow
Identify anode/cathode and oxidation/reduction in a cell
Predict cell voltage from metal reactivity differences
Explain electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds (selective discharge)
Give real applications: electroplating, aluminium extraction, rechargeable cells
g10-chemistry-uc4-t2.simple: Redox = electron transfer (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). GALVANIC CELL: put two DIFFERENT metals in an electrolyte and connect them — the more reactive metal WANTS to lose electrons more, so electrons flow through the wire from it (anode, oxidised, dissolves) to the other (cathode, where reduction happens). That wire flow = electricity. Bigger reactivity gap → bigger voltage (Mg-Cu ≈ 1.6 V; Zn-Cu ≈ 1.1 V; two identical metals → 0 V). Several cells in series = a BATTERY. ELECTROLYSIS runs it backwards: push current IN to force a reaction that won't happen alone. Molten NaCl: Na⁺ → sodium metal at cathode, Cl⁻ → chlorine at anode — clean split. Salt WATER: competition! H⁺ beats Na⁺ at the cathode (hydrogen gas), and at the anode halide-vs-hydroxide rules decide (chlorine from concentrated brine, oxygen from dilute). Uses: electroplating (thin shiny/protective metal coat), aluminium from molten alumina, recharging batteries (electrolysis ON DEMAND), purifying copper.
g10-chemistry-uc4-t2.detailed:
Simple cell anatomy: Two electrodes (different metals) + electrolyte (ion-conducting solution) + wire + voltmeter. The more reactive metal (higher in the series — Unit 5) oxidises: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (anode, negative in a galvanic cell, loses mass). Electrons travel the wire (current!) to the copper cathode, where solution cations reduce: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (copper deposits, cathode gains mass). Ions complete the circuit inside: anions → anode, cations → cathode. Salt bridge (or porous pot) keeps solutions neutral in bigger cells. Voltage = the reactivity GAP's push; standard values: Zn-Cu 1.10 V, Mg-Cu 1.61 V, Fe-Cu 0.78 V. Cells in SERIES add voltages (3 × 1.5 V AA = 4.5 V torch); in parallel they add capacity, not voltage.

Electrolysis rules (selective discharge): Electrodes: cathode (−) attracts cations, anode (+) attracts anions. MOLTEN salt: only two ions exist → each discharges simply (molten PbBr₂ → Pb + Br₂). AQUEOUS: water adds H⁺ and OH⁻ to the party — CATHODE: less reactive cation wins (H⁺ beats Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺; but Cu²⁺, Ag⁺ beat H⁺ → copper/silver plate out). ANODE: if halide concentrated → halogen (Cl₂ from brine); otherwise OH⁻ discharges → O₂. Half-equations: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Electrode material matters: inert graphite/platinum; reactive anodes dissolve themselves (electroplating, Cu purification).

Applications with numbers: Electroplating: object = cathode, plating metal = anode (replenishes solution), salt of plating metal = electrolyte (AgNO₃ for silver, CuSO₄ for copper). Aluminium (Hall-Héroult): alumina dissolved in molten cryolite (melts the mix at ~950 °C not 2050 °C — huge energy saving), carbon-lined cells, C anodes consumed by O₂ → CO₂ (topped up); one tonne Al ≈ 15 MWh — recycling saves ~95% of that. Copper purification: impure anode dissolves, pure Cu plates cathode, precious metals fall as sludge (anode mud = gold/silver recovery). Rechargeable cells: reversible galvanic — external current runs the chemistry backwards (lead-acid, Li-ion — G11/everyday).

keyTerms.def: Current forced IN to drive non-spontaneous change.
Winning ion at each electrode by reactivity/concentration.
Melts alumina cheaply for aluminium cells.

formulas.name: Anode (galvanic)
formulas.meaning: Oxidation — the reactive metal dissolves, freeing electrons.
formulas.example: Zn anode loses mass over time.

formulas.name: Cathode (galvanic)
formulas.meaning: Reduction — solution ions gain electrons, plate out.

workedExamples.problem: A Zn-Cu cell and an Mg-Cu cell are built with identical electrolytes. Which has the higher voltage and why? Predict the Mg-Cu value from reactivity data (Zn-Cu = 1.10 V, Mg-Zn gap ≈ 0.6 V).
workedExamples.substitution: Mg-Cu gap = Mg-Zn + Zn-Cu ≈ 0.6 + 1.1 = 1.7 V. Mg pushes electrons harder against Cu than Zn does.
workedExamples.answer: Mg-Cu higher — the bigger the reactivity difference, the bigger the push.

workedExamples.problem: Predict the products at each electrode when dilute Na₂SO₄ solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, and write the cathode half-equation.
workedExamples.substitution: Cathode candidates: Na⁺ vs H⁺ — H⁺ wins (Na too reactive) → hydrogen gas: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode candidates: SO₄²⁻ vs OH⁻ — sulfate never discharges in water → OH⁻ → oxygen gas: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.
workedExamples.calculation: Net effect: water decomposed (2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂); Na₂SO₄ just carries current — H₂:O₂ volume ratio 2:1.
workedExamples.answer: H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode — electrolysis of water wearing a salt costume.

workedExamples.problem: Design an electroplating cell to coat a steel spoon with silver. Specify cathode, anode, electrolyte, and what happens to the anode's mass.
workedExamples.substitution: Cathode: cleaned spoon (grease breaks adhesion). Anode: pure silver bar. Electrolyte: AgNO₃ (or silver-cyanide complex industrially). Cathode: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (spoon gains mass). Anode: Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻ (silver dissolves, REPLACING plated Ag⁺ — anode mass falls exactly as spoon mass rises).
workedExamples.calculation: Current × time controls thickness (Faraday's law — G11 preview).
workedExamples.answer: Silver migrates anode → solution → spoon; the anode is the fuel tank.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why aluminium extraction melts alumina in cryolite instead of pure alumina, and why the carbon anodes must be continuously replaced.
workedExamples.substitution: Pure Al₂O₃ melts at 2050 °C — absurd energy cost; dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) the cell runs ~950 °C. Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (molten, sinks, tapped). Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ — but the O₂ burns the CARBON anode: C + O₂ → CO₂, so anodes corrode and are topped/replaced (CO₂ is the process's carbon footprint).
workedExamples.calculation: Recycling Al needs ~5% of smelting energy — Ethiopia's scrap-aluminium re-melt is the cheaper route.
workedExamples.answer: Cryolite cuts the heat bill; oxygen eats the anodes — both are engineering compromises.

commonMistakes: Swapping anode/cathode between galvanic and electrolytic — anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction ALWAYS (only the +/- signs flip between cell types).
Thinking electrons flow through the SOLUTION — electrons ride the wire; IONS carry charge through the electrolyte.
Predicting sodium metal from aqueous NaCl electrolysis — H⁺ discharges first (Na⁺ only from MOLTEN salt).
Using two identical metals in a 'cell' and expecting voltage — the GAP drives it; same metal = 0 V.
Saying the battery 'creates electrons' — it pumps existing ones around a closed loop.
Forgetting the anode dissolves in plating/purification — students draw massless anodes.
Calling electrolysis spontaneous — it REQUIRES continuous current; stop the supply, stop the reaction.
Mixing up series vs parallel: series adds voltage (torch), parallel adds capacity (runtime).
applications: Batteries everywhere: 1.5 V cells in series (torch = 2-3 cells), phone Li-ion (rechargeable galvanic), car lead-acid.
Electroplating: silver/jewellery finishing, chrome bumpers, gold contacts — corrosion protection + beauty.
Aluminium: cans, window frames, cooking pots — one of the most electricity-hungry metals (recycling pays 95% less).
Chlor-alkali industry: brine electrolysis → Cl₂ (bleach, PVC) + NaOH (soap, paper) — a two-product backbone industry.
Copper purification: 99.99% wire-grade Cu from impure anodes; anode mud recovers gold/silver.
Hydrogen economy preview: water electrolysis (renewable-powered) makes clean fuel — the 'green hydrogen' push.
Ethiopian context: small-scale metal finishing workshops, EV charging infrastructure growth, grid hydro powering electrochemistry.
g10-chemistry-uc4-t2.summary: Galvanic: spontaneous redox → current; reactive metal = anode (oxidises, dissolves), electrons wire → cathode (reduction plates out); voltage = reactivity gap; series = battery. Electrolysis: forced backwards; molten = simple discharge; aqueous = selective (H⁺ beats Na⁺; conc halide → halogen else O₂). Uses: plating, Al (cryolite!), Cu purification, recharge.

steps: e⁻ ride the wire → current (voltmeter 1.1 V)
Cu cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (plates, gains mass)
Ions close the loop through the electrolyte
config.title: The Zinc-Copper Cell Step by Step

pairs.q: Do electrons swim through the salt solution?
pairs.a: No — electrons take the wire; IONS (Zn²⁺, SO₄²⁻) carry charge through the solution. Two different transport lanes.

pairs.q: Why does a lemon power a clock but two lemons in series do more?
pairs.a: Each cell's voltage comes from the Mg/Cu (zinc/copper) gap in citric-acid electrolyte; series stacks the pushes.

pairs.q: Your spoon plating came out flaky and grey. Two likely causes?
pairs.a: Greasy spoon (clean first — adhesion fails) or too much current (dendritic, powdery deposit instead of smooth crystal growth).

questions.q: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the:
questions.explanation: Anode = oxidation, always (OIL RIG anchor).

questions.q: Which pair gives the highest voltage?
questions.explanation: Mg-Cu has the biggest reactivity gap (~1.6 V).

questions.q: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of ____.
questions.explanation: Loss of electrons = oxidation.

questions.q: Why can't you get sodium metal by electrolyising aqueous NaCl?
questions.answer: h+ discharges first|water competes|only molten works
questions.explanation: H⁺ from water is easier to reduce than Na⁺ — you get H₂ gas; sodium needs MOLTEN NaCl with no water present.

questions.q: In electroplating silver, the object being plated is the:
questions.explanation: Cathode attracts Ag⁺ which reduces onto it.

questions.q: Pick the correct electron path in a Zn-Cu cell:
options: Zn → wire → Cu; ions in solution
questions.explanation: Electrons: anode (Zn) through wire to cathode (Cu); ions handle the solution leg.

questions.q: Cells connected in series add their voltages.
questions.explanation: 3 × 1.5 V = 4.5 V — that's how torch batteries stack.

questions.q: The mineral additive that lets alumina melt at ~950 °C is ____.
questions.explanation: Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) — the aluminium industry's energy saver.

questions.q: A torch needs 4.5 V from 1.5 V cells in series. How many cells?
At a carbon anode in the aluminium cell, why must the anode be replaced regularly?
questions.explanation: O²⁻ discharges to O₂ which reacts with the carbon anode → CO₂ — the electrode is consumed by its own product.
